_comment: Baseline-managed fragment merged into a target repo's .claude/settings.json by install.sh. Hook commands all point under .claude/hooks/baseline/ so they never collide with a repo's own hooks, and the merge is idempotent (it replaces any existing entry whose command references /.claude/hooks/baseline/). permissions.deny is unioned with whatever the repo already denies; the repo's allow list is left untouched. Every _comment* key in this file is stripped by lib/merge_settings.py and never reaches the consumer's settings.json. If you change the deny entries here, update EXPECTED_DENY in modules/config-guard.sh too (tests/policy-change-gate.sh enforces a fixture update).
_comment_matchers: The shell matchers are "Bash|PowerShell" because the PowerShell tool is default-on on Windows and, on a Windows host without Git Bash, Claude Code does not register the Bash tool at all - a hook matching only "Bash" would never fire there. Matchers are regex, so the alternation is the documented form (hooks reference: 'Match Bash|PowerShell in hooks that inspect shell commands'). NOTE the residual gap this does not close: the hook command itself is `bash "...command-guard.sh"`, so on a Windows box with no bash on PATH the hook is invoked and fails to launch, and Claude Code treats a hook that never launches as fail-open. On such a host the permissions.deny entries below - which the CLI enforces itself, with no shell involved - are the only control that actually runs.

hooks._comment_configchange: Two ConfigChange groups, not one: the documented matcher values are the config SOURCE (user_settings, project_settings, local_settings, policy_settings, skills), and .claude/settings.local.json - which overrides .claude/settings.json and is the file the README tells people not to commit - arrives as local_settings. Watching project_settings alone left the higher-precedence file unobserved, so a disableAllHooks written there was neither denied nor detected. config-guard.sh must handle the local_settings source; until it does, this group is wired but inert.

permissions._comment_deny_scope: WHAT THESE RULES BIND, EXACTLY. Read()/Edit() rules bind Claude's built-in file tools AND the file commands Claude Code recognizes inside a shell command (cat, head, tail, sed, grep). They do NOT bind arbitrary subprocesses: `python -c "open('.claude/baseline.config.json','w')..."` or `node -e ...` write the file with no rule consulted. The Bash()/PowerShell() rules below close the common shell shapes the Edit() rules miss (`>` redirection, tee, cp, mv, rm, chmod, truncate) by matching the PATH TEXT rather than the verb - deny wins over allow, and a `*` in a Bash/PowerShell rule matches at any position, so any command whose text contains one of these paths is refused whatever the verb is. Understand the limit before relying on it: this is a TEXT match on the command string. `cd .claude && sed -i s/block/warn/ baseline.config.json`, `sed -i ... "$CFG"`, or any other spelling of the same file does not contain the literal path and is NOT caught here - those depend on command-guard's tamper rule, which in turn depends on the hook actually launching. Treat the pair as defense in depth, not as a boundary. Deliberate side effect: these rules also refuse READ-ONLY shell access to the same paths (`cat .claude/settings.json`, `git add .claude/settings.json`). That is intended - posture is reported by tools/baseline-status.sh, and a verb-scoped rule would have to enumerate write verbs and would silently miss the next one.
permissions._comment_deny_powershell: Why the PowerShell block is coarser than command-guard. (1) Remove-Item is denied outright rather than only in its `-Recurse -Force` form: rules match text, and PowerShell accepts those flags in any order, abbreviated (-Rec), or before the path - a pattern targeting one spelling would be a rule that only appears to work. A repo that genuinely needs shell deletion must remove this entry deliberately; a deny cannot be re-opened by an allow rule. (2) The alias entries are not redundant with the cmdlet entries: a rule written for a cmdlet also matches that cmdlet's aliases, but under PowerShell 7 `curl`/`wget` are NOT aliases of Invoke-WebRequest - they resolve to native curl.exe/wget.exe, which alias matching cannot reach, hence the explicit and .exe forms. (3) This is a floor, not parity with command-guard: it covers destructive deletion, remote fetch, Invoke-Expression and force-push only. Everything else on the PowerShell side (git reset --hard, +refspec force pushes, a download cradle under another binary name) is matched by command-guard, which needs bash on PATH to run at all.
